claim: The Claude Code team says it does not improve reviews by stacking more reviewers: adding a second, more expensive reviewer on top of the primary one is often worse than tuning the primary reviewer with a REVIEW.md that says what to look for in this code.
why: The source states the preference and the tuning alternative but gives no measurement behind it.
check: If a setup adds a second, more expensive reviewer, check whether it tried tuning the primary reviewer's REVIEW.md for the code first.
quote: We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary.

claim: In the Claude Code team's review flow, several agents look for bugs in parallel, a separate group votes on each finding, only findings with enough agreement are posted, and findings solely about style, diagnostics or cleanup are dropped.
why: The team A/B tested the filters on its own PRs before keeping them.
check: For a review pipeline that votes on findings before posting, check whether it tests the filter on its own PRs for noise and lost bugs.
quote: Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them.

claim: An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely: on one Claude Code CLI PR the loop ran more than fifty rounds overnight, and about 59% of what the reviewer flagged on later passes was code that had been there since its first pass.
why: The team found that later rounds mostly uncovered more old bugs and says running several passes by default made the loop worse, though extra passes can be worthwhile on risky changes.
check: Check whether a review loop has a round cap and a convergence metric; an uncapped author-reviewer loop is a cost finding.
quote:
One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it.

When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.

claim: To make review converge, the Claude Code team caps review at three rounds, then asks the author to reconsider the approach, re-reviews only the new diff after the first few passes, flags the class of bug, avoids reposting findings and tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall.
why: The source reports fewer review rounds per internal PR after these changes (shown in a figure, no number in text).
check: Look for a round cap to limit automated re-review and check whether the loop re-reviews only the new diff after the first few passes and tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall.
quote:
The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review:

A round cap. After three rounds, the reviewer asks the author to step back and reconsider the approach.

Diff-only re-review after the first few passes.

Flag the class of bug, so the author fixes every instance, not one line.

No repeats of findings already posted.

claim: To measure reviewer noise, Anthropic sorts every reviewer comment by how the PR author responded (fixed it, said it was wrong, said it was intentional, decided it did not matter) and also runs the reviewer on PRs known to be clean, counting reports that would have led someone to a harmful change.
why: Catching more bugs is easy if flagging many non-bugs is tolerated, so a separate false-positive check is needed; the written priority is real bugs first, fewer review rounds second.
check: Check whether a reviewer eval measures noise as well as recall, for example by recording author responses and counting potentially harmful findings on known-clean PRs.
quote: We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change.

claim: False positives cost more when the author is an agent: a person waves off a nit in seconds, while an agent fixes it, producing another commit and another review round.
why: The source uses this to justify measuring noise and capping rounds.
check: In an agent-authored workflow, check whether reviewer nits lead to unnecessary fixes, commits and review rounds.
quote: Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.

claim: In the Claude Code team's review flow, any open finding from the bug or security review blocks merge, and the author can resolve a finding by fixing it or closing the thread with a short reason, with a later commit that fixes the issue clearing it automatically.
why: Closing a finding with a reason lets the author clear a false positive while keeping unresolved findings blocking.
check: Check whether a blocking AI review gate lets the author dismiss a false positive with a reason.
quote:
Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own.

claim: Anthropic runs its reviewer daily against past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts and bugs confirmed by engineers who know the code, and recommends rescoring the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.
why: Scoring each reviewer change on the full incident set shows whether it still catches past bugs.
check: Check whether the reviewer was scored on the team's own past incidents and rescored after changes to its prompts, tools or model.
quote: Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.

claim: The Code Review team scores recall separately for raw findings, after the verification stage, and for the final review, so it can see whether the pipeline loses bugs it had already found; a single end-to-end score hides that.
why: A verifier or filter stage can silently drop real bugs, which one combined number cannot reveal.
check: If a review pipeline has a verification or filter stage, check that recall was measured before and after it; absence means a lossy stage may be unobserved.
quote: They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.

claim: Anthropic’s Code Review eval recreates the repo as it was at review time, supplies a one-sentence bug answer key, and gives points only to findings that correctly describe the bug.
why: Grading against the actual bug checks whether the reviewer found what went wrong.
check: Check that each evaluation case uses the review-time repo state and scores findings against a bug-specific answer key.
quote: They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points.

claim: The Claude Code team audits its reviewers over time by tracking how many merged changes were reverted, how many a maintainer rejected before merge, and a size-matched subset of changes that stayed clean, and tunes recall only up to the point where the next gain would be overfitting to the eval.
why: Reverts, maintainer rejections and clean changes give the team outcome evidence for evaluating its reviewer.
check: Ask whether a setup tracks reverts or rejections of reviewed changes; a reviewer judged only by its own comment counts has no outcome signal.
quote: We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

claim: Acceptance criteria and reviewer rules must live where the change under review cannot edit them: Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch, never from the pull request, because a change that can modify its own check makes the check broken.
why: A change that can rewrite the rule that judges it can pass itself.
check: Check which version of REVIEW.md or other acceptance rules actually judges the change and flag a gate if the change under review can alter the rules it will be judged by.
quote: If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes.

claim: Code owners use REVIEW.md to tell the Claude Code reviewer what failure looks like in their part of the code.
why: The Claude Code team uses REVIEW.md for local review criteria alongside the project guidance every review loads from CLAUDE.md.
check: Check for a short REVIEW.md with local failure criteria, a cap on nits, paths to skip, file-and-line evidence, and a summary that starts with a count and explicitly says when there is nothing to fix.
quote: REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence

claim: The Claude Code team keeps a reliability checklist of 39 items, each with a trigger readable from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it; Claude reads the diff and runs only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10.
why: Triggered items spare people from memorizing past outages without running every check on every change.
check: For recurring reliability checks, look for triggers Claude can read from the diff and references to the incidents or PRs behind them.
quote: We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it.

claim: When a review misses something, the Claude Code team asks what the model did not have in front of it and puts the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check; when the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, they fix it at the source (the skill, a lint rule, or an instruction file).
why: Filling a gap in the instructions or adding a check gives Claude something it lacked when review missed the issue.
check: Check whether repeated review findings were ever promoted into a lint rule, skill or instruction file; the same finding recurring in review after review is a finding.
quote: When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check.

claim: The Claude Code team replays three bug finders on a known-incident PR and counts the bug as detectable if at least two find it.
why: The replay gives the team a way to tell which known bugs its reviewers can detect.
check: When a known bug is missed on a small diff, check whether the team recorded that gap as a candidate REVIEW.md rule.
quote: The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.

claim: In Anthropic's internal testing on structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude's work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.
why: Anthropic cites the structured file-generation result as evidence that giving agents a way to verify their output can improve quality.
check: When evaluating a grader-based loop, check the gain on the setup's own tasks against its standard prompting loop.
quote: having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

claim: Rubrics in Claude Managed Agents (beta) verify outcomes against a rubric using a separate grader agent, and failures loop back for rework automatically.
why: The managed rubric uses a separate grader agent to judge the outcome and sends failed work back for rework.
check: In a Claude Managed Agents setup with a custom grader loop, check whether the managed rubric's separate grading and automatic rework cover the same need.
quote: Rubrics in Claude Managed Agents (beta): A managed agentic service that allows you to verify outcomes against a rubric using a separate grader agent. Failures loop back for rework automatically.

claim: Anthropic recommends deterministic graders where possible, LLM graders where necessary or for flexibility, and human graders judiciously for validation; model-based graders are non-deterministic, more expensive than code and require calibration against human graders.
why: Code graders are fast, cheap, objective and reproducible but brittle to valid variations, while model graders capture nuance at the cost of calibration.
check: Check whether the eval uses deterministic graders for criteria code can decide and reserves model grading for criteria that need it or benefit from extra flexibility.
quote: We recommend choosing deterministic graders where possible, LLM graders where necessary or for additional flexibility, and using human graders judiciously for additional validation.

claim: When /claude-api build-eval proposes the cheapest suitable grader, it uses code checks for constrained outputs and defaults to an LLM judge for open-ended outputs with clear quality criteria.
why: A code check is cheap when the valid outputs are constrained, while a model judge can apply clear criteria across many valid answers.
check: Check that the selected grader fits the output space, such as a schema check for constrained JSON.
quote:
Claude proposes the cheapest grader that fits your application’s output:

Programmatic verification: If the output possibilities are constrained, it uses a code based check (exact match, a label from a fixed set, JSON that matches a schema, tests that pass).

LLM-as-judge: It will default to this type of check if the output space is open-ended, with many valid answers but clear quality criteria.

claim: In /claude-api build-eval, Claude grades a small sample and asks the user which cases they would have scored differently.
why: Anthropic recommends reading a sample of scored transcripts because scoring failures are among the most common causes of eval misconfiguration.
check: Check that the user reviewed sample scores and the associated transcripts before trusting the evaluator.
quote: Claude grades a handful of cases and asks whether you would have scored any of them differently (Figure 4). In general, it is important to read a sample of scored transcripts before believing your evaluator; scoring failures are among the most common ways an evaluation is misconfigured.

claim: Anthropic recommends calibrating LLM judges closely against human experts and giving them a way to return Unknown when information is insufficient, says structured rubrics with separate judges for each dimension can help, and says occasional human review is sufficient once the system is robust.
why: The source says the Unknown option avoids hallucinated verdicts and that vague rubrics produce inconsistent judgments.
check: Check whether the judge was calibrated against human experts and can abstain when information is insufficient, and consider isolated per-dimension grading if a multidimensional rubric needs it.
quote: To avoid hallucinations, give the LLM a way out, like providing an instruction to return “Unknown” when it doesn’t have enough information. It can also help to create clear, structured rubrics to grade each dimension of a task, and then grade each dimension with an isolated LLM-as-judge rather than using one to grade all dimensions.

claim: On CORE-Bench, Opus 4.5 initially scored 42% amid rigid grading that penalized a rounded answer, ambiguous task specs and irreproducible stochastic tasks, then scored 95% after bugs were fixed and a less constrained scaffold was used.
why: The source's point is that even sophisticated teams miss grading bugs, and that METR found similar misconfigured tasks that penalized models for following the stated instructions.
check: When an eval or reviewer score looks low, inspect the grader and task specs for rigidity and ambiguity before concluding the model is weak.
quote: Opus 4.5 initially scored 42% on CORE-Bench, until an Anthropic researcher found multiple issues: rigid grading that penalized “96.12” when expecting “96.124991…”, ambiguous task specs, and stochastic tasks that were impossible to reproduce exactly. After fixing bugs and using a less constrained scaffold, Opus 4.5’s score jumped to 95%.

claim: pass@k (at least one success in k tries) rises with k while pass^k (all k trials succeed) falls: a 75% per-trial success rate gives about 42% for three consecutive passes, so use pass^k for agents where consistency matters and pass@k where one success is enough.
why: The metrics agree at k=1 and diverge as the number of trials grows because one measures at least one success and the other measures consistent success.
check: If a setup claims a verification step or agent is reliable from a single passing run, check how many trials back that claim; for repeated-use agents one pass is weak evidence.
quote: If your agent has a 75% per-trial success rate and you run 3 trials, the probability of passing all three is (0.75)³ ≈ 42%. This metric especially matters for customer-facing agents where users expect reliable behavior every time.

claim: Anthropic says 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures are a great start for an agent eval because changes often have a large enough effect for small samples early in development, while more mature agents may need larger and harder evals to detect smaller effects.
why: Teams delay evals believing they need hundreds of tasks, and evals get harder to build the longer you wait.
check: Do not flag a small, failure-derived eval set as inadequate for an early-stage agent; do flag one that is too small to detect the effect a mature agent's change is expected to have.
quote: 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start. After all, in early agent development, each change to the system often has a clear, noticeable impact, and this large effect size means small sample sizes suffice.

claim: Shared state between eval trials can inflate scores: in some internal Anthropic evals Claude gained an unfair advantage by examining the git history from previous trials, so each trial should start from a clean environment.
why: Leftover files, cached data and exhausted resources also cause correlated failures that are infrastructure flakiness, not agent performance.
check: Check that eval trials start from a clean environment and that shared state such as earlier trials' files, caches or git history cannot skew the results.
quote: in some internal evals we observed Claude gaining an unfair advantage on some tasks by examining the git history from previous trials.

claim: Capability evals should start at a low pass rate to give a hill to climb, while regression evals should sit near 100%; a capability eval with a high pass rate can graduate into the regression suite, and a decline in a regression score signals something broke.
why: The two answer different questions: what can the agent do well, versus does it still handle everything it used to.
check: Check that capability and regression results can be read separately so declines in previously reliable behavior are visible.
quote: Regression evals ask, “Does the agent still handle all the tasks it used to?” and should have a nearly 100% pass rate. They protect against backsliding, as a decline in score signals that something is broken and needs to be improved.

claim: Anthropic describes agent evaluation as layers in the Swiss Cheese Model, with effective teams combining automated evals for fast iteration, production monitoring for ground truth and periodic human review for calibration.
why: Evaluation methods catch different failures, so one layer can catch failures that slip through another.
check: Check whether production monitoring and periodic human review fill the gaps left by automated agent evals.
quote:
Like the Swiss Cheese Model from safety engineering, no single evaluation layer catches every issue. With multiple methods combined, failures that slip through one layer are caught by another.
The most effective teams combine these methods: automated evals for fast iteration, production monitoring for ground truth, and periodic human review for calibration.

claim: In the Claude Code team’s approval process, low-risk changes can clear without a person once automated review and security checks pass, provided the author is trusted and no extra human approval applies.
why: The change sets the risk tier, and a second classifier can still require another person on a change whose tier allows automated clearance.
check: Check that automated clearance is limited to trusted authors and still requires a person for owner-designated sensitive paths, CI workflows or changes the second classifier flags.
quote: LowDocs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are green

claim: Code Review depth is set per repo as Quick, Standard or Deep, and Anthropic says Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time, so review effort should match risk: a quick pass on routine changes and a deep one where a missed bug is expensive.
why: Anthropic reports that after the research preview launch the share of internal PRs with substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%, with most PRs over 1,000 lines getting findings and most small ones coming back clean.
check: Check whether the repo's Code Review depth matches the risk of its changes and whether catching a missed bug would justify the extra time for Deep review.
quote: Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

claim: The Claude Code team measures human review time with human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments and how long a PR waits on a person, and treats revert and incident rates as the guardrail: if they rise, human time has only been moved, not saved.
why: Over June to September, merged PRs to Claude Code more than doubled while the share reverted fell by more than 40 percent.
check: Check that a proposal to cut review or add automated review names both a cost metric (human time) and a guardrail (reverts, incidents); one without the other is a finding.
quote: Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

claim: The Claude Code team says that if you can focus on only one test type it should be end-to-end, because E2E tests are hard to fool (the whole feature works or it does not), have definitive done criteria, and catch what unit tests miss when both the agent and the unit test misunderstand the full task.
why: A unit test can pass while the feature is broken because the agent and the test share the same misunderstanding.
check: When a team can invest in only one kind of test for an agent-written feature, check whether it exercises the full user flow on the running system.
quote: If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end.

claim: Flaky tests train the agent to rerun tests when the code needs a fix, and slow tests make it run fewer tests across batches, which can make failures harder to pinpoint, so heavier tests are best run before changes are committed.
why: The Claude Code team forbids Claude from skipping flaky tests, adding sleeps or retrying until they pass, and has it delete the test with a written reason if it cannot find the root cause.
check: Check the test suite and instructions for flaky tests and for any allowance to retry, skip or sleep around failures; a flaky test the agent can paper over is a finding.
quote: If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes.

claim: In the Claude Code team's verification loop, Claude runs the checks and tries to fix failures, and if a check is still failing after three rounds Claude stops and brings in a human.
why: Nobody can read every change, so persistent failure is used as the signal for what needs a person.
check: Check that an automated fix-and-verify loop has an explicit round limit and an escalation to a human; an unbounded retry loop is a finding.
quote: If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

claim: The Claude Code team recommends starting new verification gates in observe mode, which logs the actions the gate would have blocked.
why: The team reviews would-be blocks for false positives before enforcement affects anyone.
check: Check that a new verification gate starts by logging would-be blocks for review before moving to enforce mode.
quote: Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.

claim: The Claude Code team has Claude run tests, the build and the linter before opening a pull request, and suggests a hook that runs tests when Claude finishes or a /goal of a passing test suite as ways to enforce test execution.
why: Pushing before testing locally burns shared review and CI capacity.
check: Check whether Claude runs the tests, build and linter before opening a pull request, and whether a hook or /goal is configured if the setup uses one to enforce testing.
quote: On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite.

claim: Verification rules need pruning: the Claude Code team says test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so they tidy them up on a routine, and they prune lessons so those stay worth running.
why: The team prunes verification lessons so the checks stay worth running.
check: Check whether test suites, verification steps and Markdown rules are pruned when they no longer earn their place.
quote: Rules need cleaning up too.

claim: Property tests such as round-trip encoding, invariants, idempotency and equivalence to a naive correct version exercise generated edge cases outside the code author's assumptions and are particularly helpful in rewrites where the spec has drifted from production behavior.
why: Libraries such as fast-check, Hypothesis and proptest generate thousands of inputs trying to disprove a statement you believe cannot fail.
check: For a rewrite with a spec that has drifted from production behavior, check whether property-based tests exercise edge cases beyond those anticipated by the code author.
quote: Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that aren’t created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code.

claim: For a large migration expected to preserve functionality, differential tests compare the old and new systems on the same randomly generated inputs or sample of production traffic after normalizing irrelevant differences such as whitespace and accounting for approved changes.
why: The old system acts as the oracle when the spec is unreliable.
check: For a migration expected to preserve functionality, check for an old-versus-new comparison on real or random inputs that accounts for approved changes and investigates unexpected differences.
quote:
where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.

The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic.

claim: Verification skills had the most measurable impact on Claude’s output quality within the Claude Code team, which says a week of engineering time to improve them can be worthwhile.
why: The team suggests recording video to show exactly what Claude tested or adding assertions to check state at each step.
check: Check whether verification skills exercise the product workflow and collect evidence through recordings or programmatic state checks.
quote: Verification skills have had the most measurable impact on Claude’s output quality internally. It can be worth having an engineer spend a week just making your verification skills excellent.

claim: To codify how to start the app or simulator, create a skill called verify under .claude/skills/ in the repo as close to the relevant code as possible, make it fast and reliable by iterating and stress-testing it as the smoke-test harness, and Claude knows to use it before committing changes.
why: The source says giving Claude an end-to-end smoke test makes it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, and that this is how nearly all changes are tested at Anthropic.
check: Check whether the verify skill is fast and reliable, and whether it has been stress-tested as an end-to-end smoke test.
quote: To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.

claim: Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, estimates that giving Claude a way to verify its work makes the final result two to three times better and calls it probably the most important thing for good results; this is a creator's estimate, not a reported measurement.
why: He adds that verification looks different per domain, from a bash command to a test suite to a browser or phone simulator.
check: Treat the 2-3x figure as directional only; the auditor should check whether a verification path exists for the domain, not quote the figure as evidence.
quote: He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better

claim: The Claude Code team's internal adversarial-review skill spawns a fresh-context subagent to critique, implements fixes and iterates until findings become nitpicks.
why: The skill uses fresh context for the critique and the severity of remaining findings as its stopping criterion.
check: If a setup uses the adversarial-review pattern, check whether the critique has fresh context and whether the loop stops once the remaining findings are nitpicks.
quote: adversarial-review — spawns a fresh-eyes subagent to critique, implements fixes, iterates until findings degrade to nitpicks

claim: Anthropic measures skill usage with a PreToolUse hook that logs skill invocations within the company, which lets it find skills that are popular or undertriggering compared with expectations.
why: Comparing logged invocations with expectations helps the team identify undertriggering skills.
check: Check whether skill invocations can be measured against expected usage before concluding a skill is undertriggering.
quote: we use a PreToolUse hook that lets us log skill usage within the company

claim: The highest-signal content in a skill is its Gotchas section, built from the failure points Claude actually hits and updated over time; a skill that restates what Claude would do by default adds context without adding value.
why: The source says most of its best skills began as a few lines and a single gotcha, then grew as people added edge cases Claude hit.
check: Check skills for a gotchas section grounded in real failures; a long skill of generic advice with no gotchas is a finding.
quote: The highest-signal content in any skill is the Gotchas section.

claim: Anthropic's team found its internal skills cluster into nine categories and says the best skills fit cleanly into one while skills that try to do too much straddle several and confuse the agent.
why: The categories are library and API reference, product verification, data fetching, business process automation, code scaffolding, code quality and review, CI/CD, runbooks and infrastructure operations.
check: Check whether a broad skill combines unrelated jobs in ways that confuse the agent, using the categories to identify possible splits.
quote: The best skills fit cleanly into one; the ones that try to do too much straddle several and confuse the agent.

claim: A check can be embedded in a producing skill only if the SKILL.md is editable: built-in skills and plugin-managed skills that get overwritten on update are off-limits, and for those you chain by writing a wrapper skill that invokes the original and then the verification skill.
why: Embedding a one-line check in the producing skill makes the workflow run it without being asked; verify by invoking the skill on a fresh task and confirming the step runs.
check: Check that an appended verification step does not live in a plugin-managed skill file that an update will overwrite.
quote: Built-in skills and plugin-managed skills (the kind that get overwritten on update) are off-limits for this pattern; for those, chain instead.

claim: Anthropic recommends testing chained verification skills before rolling them out broadly because the chain can increase token spend.
why: Chaining trades flexibility for automation, so independent steps can stay standalone when they sometimes need to run separately.
check: Check the token spend of a chain such as /code-review, /simplify and /verify before broad deployment.
quote: Chained verification loops can increase token spend, so it's best to test these loops before deploying them broadly.

claim: List the exact build and test commands in CLAUDE.md so Claude can use them when verifying changes, and turn recurring manual checks into verification loops where Claude cannot infer the steps from deterministic signals.
why: Claude already checks some of its work by observing deterministic signals from type checkers, linters, tests and runtime errors.
check: Check whether CLAUDE.md names the actual build and test commands so Claude can run them without inferring them.
quote: A good practice is to list your exact build and test commands in CLAUDE.md so Claude doesn't have to infer them.

claim: Anthropic’s hillclimb reverts a patch when its training score improves but its held-out test score stays flat.
why: A gain limited to the training cases can indicate overfitting to the eval.
check: Check that the eval was randomly split into train and test sets, and that patches with train-only gains are reverted.
quote: if the train set improves but the test set is flat, Claude suspects overfitting and reverts the patch.

claim: When hillclimbing, the hillclimber must never paste failure content from transcripts into the prompt, and must keep answers structurally out of the model's reach, because models can reward hack by finding the answers to evaluations.
why: Keeping failure content out of prompts and answers out of the evaluated model's reach reduces opportunities for the evaluation to leak into the harness.
check: Check whether the hillclimber copied failure content from eval transcripts into the prompt or left eval answers accessible to the model being evaluated.
quote: If the hillclimber reads the failing transcripts, it should never paste the failure content into the prompt.

claim: Choose hillclimbing surfaces that are cheap to change and whose effects show up in the eval score, such as prompts or skills tuned against a directly related metric like skill triggering, and use a well-scoped objective such as reducing cost while holding performance steady on a saturated eval.
why: Open-ended harness changes or near-saturated evals tend to stall, and when the baseline already scores about 95% or higher the skill warns that the hillclimb should aim at cost or latency instead of quality.
check: Check whether the eval metric is directly tied to the surface being edited and whether the objective accounts for the eval's available headroom.
quote: One generally strong objective across various efforts is cost: even if an evaluation is saturated, you can ask Claude to find ways to reduce cost while keeping performance at parity.

claim: When a hillclimb score stalls for two or three rounds, Anthropic’s workflow diagnoses each remaining training failure before making more edits.
why: Diagnosing failures can expose ambiguous cases, harness errors or run-to-run variance.
check: Check for flawed tasks or graders when fixes to obvious content gaps produce no improvement, such as a grader expecting a chain of errors when a task asked for one error type.
quote: When the score stalls for two or three rounds, Claude reads each remaining train failure and sorts it by cause. It does the same early if no single fix could gain more than the eval's noise, and suggests more repetitions or cases, rather than spending rounds on changes too small to measure. This step can catch ambiguous evaluation cases, harness errors, or run-to-run variance.

claim: On Anthropic’s claude-api skill eval, performance reached 80% after Claude mapped old API forms to their replacements in a table and moved fixed-budget thinking warnings above the C# and Java examples.
why: Claude kept writing older API forms even though the skill already covered the current ones.
check: When Claude keeps emitting obsolete API forms, check for a replacement table near the top of the skill and warnings before affected examples, such as those for adaptive thinking.
quote: remembered to the current ones: for example, from extended thinking with a fixed token budget, which the API now rejects on recent Opus models, to adaptive thinking, and from older versions of the web search and web fetch tools to the current ones. It also moved the C# and Java warnings against fixed-budget thinking above their adaptive-thinking examples. This improved performance to 80%.

claim: A well-designed eval should typically score better with more capable models or higher effort while leaving passable headroom below 100% at the highest capability and effort, and a lack of improvement can point to ambiguous tasks or a miscalibrated grader while inconsistent effort can add variance.
why: A task that fails every run regardless of replicates is a common tell of an impossible or ambiguous task.
check: Compare eval scores across models or effort levels and inspect tasks and graders if stronger settings do not help.
quote: More capable models and higher effort levels typically should perform better on an evaluation. If they don’t, ambiguous tasks or a miscalibrated grader often are hobbling performance.

claim: Pick hard eval cases a human can explain as hard, since choosing cases solely because today's model fails them can measure one model's failure patterns, and check whether relying solely on user traffic skews the set easy because users sometimes try what they expect to work.
why: A useful test is to be able to say why a task is hard before including it.
check: Check whether hard eval cases have a reason for inclusion beyond current-model failure and whether user-traffic cases cover the difficulty the application needs.
quote: If you pick cases because today's model fails them, you are sampling the valleys of one model's capability surface

claim: Across Anthropic's Terminal-Bench 3.0 runs, higher effort tended to reduce missed-edge-case failures without fixing a wrong approach, with Fable 5.1 going from 1/5 at low to 5/5 at xhigh on the HTML sanitizer task and Opus 5.5 showing gains on selected edge-case-heavy tasks.
why: At low effort attempts wrote a filter in about one pass and tested one hand-written page, while a high-effort run adversarially reviewed its draft, ran an XSS suite and wrote a fuzzer, which is extra verification behavior.
check: When considering higher effort, check whether failures come from missed edge cases that more verification could catch or from an approach that needs to change.
quote: increasing effort tends to reduce failures due to missing edgecases (purple blocks), but does not fix when the model has the wrong approach (blue blocks).

claim: In Anthropic's Terminal-Bench 3.0 runs, Fable 5.1's pass rate from pooled low to pooled top effort went from 64% to 87% in security, 34% to 75% in hardware, 54% to 73% in ML, 41% to 61% in science, 43% to 56% in software, 18% to 30% in media and 12% to 22% in operations.
why: The source's footnote says these are internal runs, 5 attempts per task, with production safety interventions off for Fable 5.1 and security tasks run without internet access, so counts will not match the public leaderboard.
check: Use the category results to guide which workloads to test at higher effort and measure the gain on the setup's own tasks.
quote:
Fable 5.1, pass rate at low effort → top effort: Security 64% → 87%, Hardware 34% → 75%, ML 54% → 73%, Science 41% → 61%, Software 43% → 56%, Media 18% → 30%, Operations 12% → 22%.

FIG CPass rate. Low effort pools each model's two lowest settings, top effort its three highest, since categories are small.

claim: For Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 in Claude Code, Thariq Shihipar suggests low effort for quick interactive work, medium for routine engineering, high when verification or edge cases matter, and max for hard, fully autonomous work.
why: In his own feature-development loop, the author has Claude implement on low effort and verify and test on high.
check: Check whether the effort matches the task, such as using high effort for a bug fix where verification or edge cases matter.
quote:
Low: for when I want quick responses that are in the loop, e.g. brainstorming, sketching, easy changes

Medium: for most of my regular software engineering work, e.g. new feature implementation.

High: for work where verification is important or there are edge cases, e.g. fixing a bug in a brownfield codebase.

Max: When I want Claude to operate fully autonomously to solve difficult problems

claim: In the author's fitness-app experiment, Opus 5.5 made more choices and built out more of the underspecified app as effort rose from low at 1.5 minutes to max at 67 minutes, while models and effort levels produced more similar designs and implementations when given the detailed spec for that app.
why: The author uses low effort to get a quick starting point for iteration and observes that higher effort gets more work done while making more choices on the user's behalf.
check: For a well-specified build task, check whether higher effort improves the result enough to justify the extra time on that task.
quote:
I tried asking Claude to interview me in-depth about the fitness app and then gave that spec to be implemented by different models at different effort levels.

I found that given this spec, the models behaved much more similarly. I got designs that looked fairly similar and had similar implementations but with different details

claim: When a model falls short, Anthropic advises checking that it can verify its work, then raising effort one level, then trying the next model up at a lower effort than the smaller model used.
why: Giving a model a way to verify its work often costs less and adds less latency than raising effort.
check: Check for a way to verify the result, such as a test or build, and for trials of the next effort level and the next model at lower effort, in that order.
quote:
When a model isn't good enough for a task, take these steps in order:

Check that the model can verify its own work, with a test, a build or a script that calls the endpoint.

Raise effort one level.

Move to the next model up, starting at a lower effort level than you used on the smaller one.

claim: On Anthropic’s Terminal-Bench 3.0 runs, Opus 5.5 at high effort scored 58.9% with half the tokens of Fable 5.1 at max, which scored 58.0%.
why: Per-token price alone does not tell you what a task will cost because models can use different numbers of tokens.
check: When benchmarking Opus 5.5 against Fable 5.1, check both task scores and token usage at the chosen effort levels.
quote: on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens.

claim: On a SWE-bench Pro subset Opus 5.5 at medium scored about 2.5 points lower than high at about 70% of the cost, low scored about 8 points lower at about a third of the cost, and xhigh scored about 1.4 points higher at 2.5 times the cost of high.
why: The source uses these numbers to show effort and latency are roughly correlated and that the accuracy gained must be weighed against the extra cost and latency.
check: Compare the accuracy, cost and latency of the pinned effort level against lower-effort runs on the workload it will serve.
quote: For example, on SWE-bench Pro, Opus 5.5 at medium scored about 2.5 points lower for about 70% of the cost as the high effort setting. At low it scored about 8 points lower for about a third of the cost. At xhigh it scored about 1.4 points higher for 2.5 times the cost of high.

claim: When comparing two models, price the hardest tasks in your set as well as the typical ones, because the hardest tasks carry most of the spend: on one 20-problem search benchmark, two problems carried 43% of the spend.
why: Including hard tasks shows costs that a sample of only typical cases could miss.
check: Check that a cost comparison includes the hardest cases; a comparison on typical tasks only is incomplete.
quote: price the hardest tasks in your set as well as the typical ones, because the hardest tasks carry most of the spend. On one 20-problem search benchmark, two problems carried 43% of the spend.

claim: Anthropic recommends using smaller models such as Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 for Claude Code subagents when mistakes are cheap to spot, while keeping code edits and judgment calls with the main model.
why: A small model that misreads a search result can send the main model to the wrong file and waste tokens.
check: Check whether cheaper subagents handle tasks like finding files, running tests and reading logs, with edits and decisions staying on the main model.
quote: Keep small models on work where a mistake is cheap to spot, like finding files, running tests and reading logs. Keep code edits and judgment calls on the main model. When a small model misreads a search result, the main model opens the wrong file and spends tokens on it.

claim: In current versions of Claude Code the built-in Explore subagent runs on the session's model instead of always on Haiku, and on the Claude API that model is capped at Opus, so to keep exploration cheap you define your own subagent named Explore with model: haiku.
why: The haiku alias resolves to Haiku 5.5 on the Anthropic API (needs Claude Code v2.1.293 or later) but still to Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS.
check: Check the actual model used by built-in Explore or a custom Explore, including the Claude API's Opus cap and the provider-specific resolution of any haiku alias.
quote: In current versions of Claude Code, the built-in Explore subagent runs on your session's model instead of always running on Haiku. On the Claude API, that model is capped at Opus. To keep exploration cheap, define your own subagent named Explore with model: haiku.

claim: In Claude Code, the opusplan alias uses Opus in plan mode and Sonnet to execute the plan, including code edits.
why: The alias determines which model does the implementation work.
check: If the setup uses opusplan, check that the audit identifies Sonnet as the model making the edits.
quote: Claude Code also has the opusplan alias, which plans with Opus in plan mode and then carries out the plan with Sonnet. That puts your code edits on Sonnet.

claim: On Anthropic’s internal coding benchmark, Opus 5.5 at high with a Fable 5.1 advisor scored 90.1% at $2.92 per attempt, a 1.7-point gain at about 2.1 times the cost of Opus 5.5 alone at high.
why: The gain was at the edge of run-to-run noise and comparable to what raising effort might have bought.
check: Compare advisor gains against the executor alone at the same effort, using cost per attempt and run-to-run variance.
quote: Where it adds little: one of those pairings was an Opus 5.5 executor at high with a Fable 5.1 advisor on an internal coding benchmark. It scored 90.1% at $2.92 per attempt. That's 1.7 points over Opus 5.5 alone at high for about 2.1 times the money.

claim: On an internal defect-search benchmark of about 22 million source-code tokens, an Opus 5.5 lead with up to 25 Sonnet 5.5 workers at a time cost about a third less than Opus 5.5 alone at default effort and scored about the same.
why: For work bigger than one context window, a lead can split the work across cheaper parallel workers and merge their results.
check: When comparing a lead-and-worker setup with a single model on a large task, check score and cost against the single-model run at default effort.
quote: On an internal defect-search benchmark over about 22 million tokens of source code, an Opus 5.5 lead over Sonnet 5.5 workers, up to 25 at a time, cost about a third less than Opus 5.5 alone at its default effort. It scored about the same.

claim: Anthropic recommends keeping a multi-model setup only if it beats every single-model point on a score-versus-spend chart for your own tasks.
why: Published benchmarks help choose a starting model, while measurements on real tasks show whether mixing models improves score versus spend.
check: Check whether the multi-model setup was compared with every single-model configuration on score and spend for the team’s real tasks.
quote: Plot score against spend. Keep a multi-model setup only if it beats every single-model point on that chart.

claim: On Anthropic’s support-ticket hillclimb search set, Opus 5.5 at low scored 87.8% at 1.9 cents per ticket after a prompt audit, up from 74.4% at 4.6 cents with Opus 4.8 at high.
why: The hillclimb removed mandatory tool-call rituals, a scratchpad step and contradictory rules before trying Opus 5.5, whose token pricing also contributed to the savings.
check: When comparing model and effort settings for a workflow, check decision accuracy and token cost per case against the original setup.
quote:
It started on Opus 4.8 at default (high) effort settings with 74.4% decision accuracy on the search tickets and a token cost of 4.6 cents per ticket.

The hillclimb first audited the prompt, removing mandatory tool-call rituals, a scratchpad step, and contradictory rules. Then it tried Opus 5.5 on low effort. This cleared the baseline accuracy bar at 87.8% and cut cost to 1.9 cents per ticket

claim: Anthropic’s November 2026 price table lists Claude API input/output rates per million tokens of $2/$10 for Sonnet 5.5, $4/$20 for Opus 5.5, and $8/$40 for Fable 5.2.
why: The post compares cost per completed task because a higher price per token can still yield comparable or lower task costs.
check: Check input and output estimates against the listed rates and compare candidates by cost per completed task using their actual usage.
quote: Input / output, per million tokens$0.10 / $0.50 for prompts up to 100K tokens, $0.50 / $2.50 over 100K$2 / $10$4 / $20$8 / $40

claim: Anthropic’s Code Review eval uses stable merged changes as a control for over-flagging.
why: Stable changes help reveal whether the reviewer raises findings on changes that stayed clean.
check: Check whether the reviewer eval includes stable merged changes and measures unwanted findings on them.
quote: They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging.

claim: Anthropic’s Code Review eval keeps its tuning set separate from its fixed test set.
why: The fixed test set measures reviewer performance on changes outside the tuning set.
check: Check that the cases used to tune the reviewer are separate from the fixed test cases.
quote: Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.

claim: The Claude Code team separately checks whether its automated reviewer follows the code owners’ REVIEW.md.
why: A separate check establishes whether the reviewer follows the instructions the code owners wrote.
check: Look for a check that compares the reviewer's output with the applicable REVIEW.md instructions.
quote: REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it.

claim: In the Claude Code repo, patterns from human review comments and PR reverts qualify as potential reviewer rules if they recur in at least two PRs and are recognizable from a diff.
why: The eligibility check focuses the rules on recurring problems that reviewers can see in a diff.
check: Check that the pattern met both eligibility conditions, three agents tried to disprove it, and a human reviewed and approved it in a PR.
quote: The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

claim: For standalone LLM grading in /claude-api build-eval, the judge reads the input, output and a rubric of checkable claims, then returns a score with its reasoning.
why: A checkable rubric gives the judge explicit criteria to apply and makes its reasoning reviewable.
check: Check that standalone scores come with reasoning against checkable rubric claims.
quote: In this case, a second model reads the input, the output and a rubric written as checkable claims (not a 1-to-5 scale), and returns a score with its reasoning.

claim: When /claude-api build-eval has a baseline for LLM grading, the judge sees both entries in random order without being told which is the baseline and picks the better one.
why: Random order and a hidden baseline keep the judge from relying on which entry is the baseline.
check: Check that the pairwise judge receives both entries in random order with the baseline identity hidden.
quote: If you have a baseline to compare against, the judge instead reads both inputs in random order, without being told which is the baseline, and picks the better one.

claim: During the /claude-api build-eval baseline, Claude runs the grader twice on the same output and reports whether the verdict changed.
why: Repeating the grade on the same output lets the team detect inconsistent verdicts.
check: Check whether the baseline report compares repeated verdicts on identical output.
quote: Grader: Claude runs the grader twice on the same output, and reports whether the verdict changed.

claim: The Claude Code team’s risk tiers call for one human approval on medium-risk changes and two on high-risk changes.
why: A classifier sets the tier from the change, and some paths always require two people.
check: Check that a medium-risk change has one human approval and a high-risk change has two, with any stricter approval requirement still applied.
quote:
MediumOrdinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system promptsOne person
HighThe highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two peopleTwo people

claim: Only authors on the repository’s trusted list can use the Claude Code team’s lighter approval paths, and other authors need a second person to approve.
why: The trusted list is usually made up of the team that owns the repository.
check: Check that any change by an author outside the trusted list has the required second human approval.
quote: Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve.

claim: In the Claude Code team’s approval process, an agent’s approval never fills a slot that requires a human.
why: Automated review can clear eligible low-risk changes, while a required human approval still has to come from a person.
check: Inspect the approval records and flag any required human slot filled by an agent.
quote: An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

claim: In enforce mode, the Claude Code team’s commit gate can block a commit when the session ran neither /code-review nor /verify.
why: The team stamps commits with how they were verified, including none, so unverified commits can be queried.
check: Check that the gate uses the session’s verification history and supports off, observe and enforce modes.
quote:
We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.

Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.

Enforce mode will block the commit.

claim: The Claude Code team’s commit gate allows the next commit after it has blocked two commits in the same session.
why: The same-session bypass keeps Claude from getting stuck.
check: Check that the commit gate permits the next commit after two blocks in the same session.
quote: If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck

claim: Anthropic recommends waiting until a verification chain is stable before making it a gate on every PR.
why: Every adjustment becomes visible to the team once the gate runs on all PRs.
check: Check that the chain is stable on its author’s changes before requiring it on every PR.
quote: Hold off on PR-wide gates while the chain is still in flux; every adjustment becomes a team-visible event.

claim: Before its first hillclimb round, Claude checks whether eval noise is smaller than the smallest improvement the user would act on.
why: Chance alone can move scores enough to obscure a worthwhile improvement.
check: Check that the workflow estimates noise up front and proposes more repetitions or cases if it cannot resolve a meaningful gain.
quote: Before the first round, Claude checks that the eval's noise (how far the score can move by chance alone) is smaller than the smallest improvement you'd act on; if it isn't, it says so and suggests more repetitions or cases.

claim: Anthropic’s hillclimb reports when a measured gain is within eval noise and recommends against merging in that case.
why: The test result is reported against the baseline with confidence intervals.
check: Check whether the report identifies gains within noise and recommends against merging changes with inconclusive gains.
quote: It reports the test result against the baseline with confidence intervals (Figure 7). If the gain is within noise, it says so and recommends against merging.

claim: On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high effort scored 45.3% against 45.5% for Opus 5.5 at max, at roughly half the cost per task.
why: Anthropic cites this result when recommending testing Fable 5.2 before raising Opus 5.5 past high on a hard task.
check: When considering Opus 5.5 above high for a hard task, compare its score and cost per completed task with Fable 5.2 at a lower effort.
quote: On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high scored about level with Opus 5.5 at max (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task.

claim: In Claude Code, set a subagent’s model in its definition with values such as model: haiku or model: sonnet, or let CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL supply the default when the definition omits the model.
why: A subagent’s tokens are billed at the rate of the model it runs on.
check: Check explicit model settings in subagent definitions and the environment default for definitions that omit the model.
quote: In Claude Code, set model: haiku or model: sonnet in a subagent's definition. The CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL environment variable sets the default for subagents that don't specify a model.

claim: Anthropic recommends measuring opusplan on your own tasks before making it the Claude Code default.
why: With opusplan, Sonnet makes the edits, while the post generally recommends leaving edits with the main model.
check: Check for measurements on the team’s own tasks before it defaults to opusplan.
quote: Measure opusplan on your own tasks before you make it your default.

claim: Anthropic reports that none of the four advisor pairings in its platform cost guide clearly beat its executor alone.
why: An advisor can only help when the executor asks for advice.
check: Check whether a proposed advisor pairing beats the executor alone on the team’s own tasks.
quote: The platform's cost guide is cautious: of the four pairings in its advisor table, none clearly beat its executor alone, and an advisor can help only when the executor consults it.

claim: An advisor only helps when it adds capability the executor lacks and the executor consults it, which happens less often at low effort.
why: Most tokens bill at the executor’s rate, so any benefit depends on when the executor asks for guidance.
check: Check the executor’s advisor consult rate at the chosen effort and whether consultations add capability.
quote: The advisor helps only when it adds capability the executor lacks and the executor asks for advice, which it does less often at low effort.

claim: Anthropic advises skipping Claude Managed Agents orchestration when the work fits in one context window or is a single chain of dependent steps.
why: For those tasks, planning and merging cost more than orchestration saves.
check: Check whether the work exceeds a single context window and has independent pieces before using a coordinator and workers.
quote: On the Claude Platform, multiagent orchestration in Claude Managed Agents gives you a coordinator agent and a roster of workers. Skip it for one chain of dependent steps or for work that fits in one context window. There, the planning and merging cost more than they save.

claim: Anthropic recommends testing each candidate model at two or three effort levels in separate sessions so the runs do not share a cache.
why: Separate sessions keep one run’s cache from influencing another.
check: Look for a sample of real tasks with outcome checks, isolated sessions for each model and effort, and per-task costs recorded from response usage.
quote:
Pull a sample of real tasks. Write an outcome check for each one, such as a passing test, a closed ticket or a correct row count.

Run each candidate model at two or three effort levels, each in its own session so that the runs don't share a cache. Record the cost of each completed task from the usage field of each response.

claim: After comparing model configurations, Anthropic recommends running the winner in shadow on a slice of real traffic before cutover.
why: Shadowing gives the team a chance to see how the chosen configuration handles real traffic before switching over.
check: Check for a shadow run on real traffic before the team cuts over to the winning configuration.
quote: Run the winner in shadow on a slice of real traffic before you cut over.

claim: On Anthropic’s support-ticket hillclimb search set, Sonnet 5 at low scored 88.9% at about 1 cent per ticket, roughly half the cost of the preceding Opus 5.5 run at low.
why: The hillclimb tested a cheaper tier after Opus 5.5 cleared the baseline accuracy bar.
check: After a candidate clears the accuracy target, check whether a cheaper model can clear it on the same evaluation.
quote: Because Opus 5.5 cleared the bar, the hillclimb then stepped down a tier to check whether a cheaper model could clear it too. Sonnet 5 on low effort scored about the same, 88.9%, at about half the cost, 1 cent per ticket (Figure 8).

claim: On Anthropic’s support-ticket hillclimb search set, prompt fixes brought Sonnet 5 to 98.9% at about the same cost as its earlier run.
why: The prompt changes added routing rules and a refund-cap cross-reference.
check: Check whether targeted prompt fixes improve decision accuracy at the same cost before moving to a higher tier.
quote: Finally, Claude improved the prompt with routing rules and a refund-cap cross-reference, bringing Sonnet 5 to 98.9% at about the same cost.

claim: On 14 held-out support tickets, Anthropic’s final Sonnet 5 setup scored 90.5% versus 78.6% for the original Opus 4.8 setup at high effort, at about one fifth of the cost.
why: The hillclimb used 30 of 44 tickets for search and reserved the other 14 for held-out evaluation.
check: Check whether the final configuration’s decision accuracy and cost were compared with the original setup on tickets excluded from tuning.
quote: On the 14 held-out tickets that the search never saw, the final configuration scored 90.5% against the original setup's 78.6%, at about one fifth of the cost.

claim: Anthropic’s November 2026 price table lists Claude API input/output rates for Haiku 5.5 of $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens for prompts up to 100K tokens and $0.50/$2.50 above 100K.
why: The table gives Haiku 5.5 two input and output price tiers based on prompt length.
check: Check that each Haiku 5.5 API request is costed using the tier for its prompt length.
quote: Input / output, per million tokens$0.10 / $0.50 for prompts up to 100K tokens, $0.50 / $2.50 over 100K

claim: Anthropic’s November 2026 price table lists Claude API cache-read rates per million tokens of $0.10 for Sonnet 5.5 and $0.20 each for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2.
why: The table lists the same cache-read rate for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 and a lower rate for Sonnet 5.5.
check: Check that the cost estimate uses the model’s listed cache-read rate for cached tokens read.
quote: Cache reads, per million tokens$0.01 up to 100K, $0.05 over 100K$0.10$0.20$0.20
